honest.heading: What Vauchi does not do
honest.item1: It does not take back what you already shared. You choose what each person sees, and you can change it or withdraw it at any time — but someone who has already read your number can remember it. Nobody can unsend.
honest.item2: It is not protection from someone dangerous. Vauchi can stop sending someone updates, quietly. It cannot make you unfindable, and we will not pretend otherwise.
honest.item3: It is not finished. Vauchi is being built in the open and the apps are not out yet. Everything here describes what we are building — and the code is public, so you can check how far it has come.
honest.item4: There is still a server in the middle. Your phone can't keep an open line to everyone you know — that would drain the battery — so updates wait at a relay until your phone next checks in. The relay holds them sealed and has no key, and the addresses it sorts by change every day, so it is never handed the list of who knows whom. It does see that something arrived. You can run your own.
honest.label: Being straight with you
honest.note: If anything on this page ever stops matching the code, the code is the truth.

why.body1: The internet handed everyone a permanent address — a number, an inbox, a profile — and then made it expensive to leave. Change one and you spend a year chasing the people who matter. Keep it, and it follows you for the rest of your life.
why.body2: People change jobs, countries, phones and names. The way we reach each other should be allowed to change too — without asking a company for permission, and without losing anyone along the way.
why.heading: Contact details were never meant to be permanent.
